key_insight: The paper provides the first quantitative, topology-based definition of churn flow by using Euler Characteristic Surfaces (ECS) and introduces an unsupervised Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) method that fuses ECS-derived kernels to discover and correct flow regimes (including updates to the Wu flow‑regime map).
problem_solved: Churn flow—an oscillatory, chaotic vertical two‑phase regime—has lacked a precise mathematical characterization for decades; this work supplies a reproducible, data-driven definition and an automated method to discover and correct regime labels in small‑diameter vertical pipes.
method: Compute Euler Characteristic Surfaces χ(s,t) from multi‑scale topological summaries of two‑phase flow time series.
Construct two complementary ECS‑based kernels: (a) temporal alignment using L1 distance on χ(s,t), and (b) amplitude statistics (scale‑wise mean, std, max, min).
Fuse kernels via unsupervised Multiple Kernel Learning to discover regimes and apply corrections to the Wu flow‑regime map.
impact: Demonstrates how topological features combined with kernel fusion enable robust, physics‑aware unsupervised discovery in complex dynamical systems—useful for ML practitioners working on time‑series clustering, domain correction, and interpretable feature design.
visual_elements: Annotated schematic of vertical two‑phase regimes (bubble, churn, slug) with an emphasis on churn flow dynamics.
Heatmap/3D surface of an Euler Characteristic Surface χ(s,t) showing scale vs. time topology changes for churn vs. other regimes.
Diagram showing the two ECS‑derived kernels feeding into an MKL fusion block and producing cluster/regime labels.
Before-and-after Wu map overlay: original Wu flow‑regime map with automated corrections and clustered regime boundaries.
paper_title: Topological Characterization of Churn Flow and Unsupervised Correction to the Wu Flow-Regime Map in Small-Diameter Vertical Pipes
paper_authors: Brady Koenig, Sushovan Majhi, Atish Mitra, Abigail Stein, Burt Todd
